strengths: Novel task formulation: First work to decode semantic, text-specific reading goals (vs. prior procedural goal classification). Well-motivated with scientific and practical value.

Rigorous experimental design: Careful cross-validation accounting for data non-i.i.d. structure, multiple generalization levels (New Participant/Text/Both), proper statistical testing with mixed effects models.
Comprehensive evaluation framework: Two-tier task difficulty, five reconstruction metrics, multiple baselines, detailed comparison of discriminative and generative approaches.
High-quality dataset: Professional eye tracking (EyeLink 1000 Plus), manually annotated critical spans, 1M+ tracked word tokens, publicly available resource for community.
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed model descriptions, hyperparameter search spaces, training procedures, and evaluation protocols enabling replication.
Thoughtful ethical considerations: Acknowledges limitations and potential harms for unreliable real-world deployment, discusses consent and user identification risks.
weaknesses: Modest performance with insufficient analysis: 49.3% accuracy (16pp above 33% chance); 57.3% on harder task (7.3pp above 50% chance). Only one qualitative example; no error analysis of which questions are harder or what patterns models exploit.

Generative models severely underperform: DalEye-LLaVA at 33.5% (chance level); DalEye-Llama reconstruction quality weak, underperformed by human baseline on BLEU/BERTScore in New Text regime. Failures not adequately explained.

Severely limited scope: Single dataset (OneStop), language (English), population (native speakers). Constrained texts (109 words, 5.8 sentences). Only multiple-choice reading comprehension questions. Unclear generalization to diverse question types and longer documents.

Limited technical novelty: Models are mostly adaptations of existing work (Haller et al. 2022, Shubi et al. 2024, LLaVA-OneVision). Main contribution is task formulation, not modeling innovation. Missing ablations on features and architecture choices.

Simple baselines fail unexpectedly: Reading-time models at chance level, contradicting prior literature on strong RT effects. Suggests suboptimal baseline design rather than demonstrating task difficulty.

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: No analysis of which eye movement features matter, what patterns models learn, or why generative approaches fail. Missing ablation studies and per-question-type breakdowns.

Questionable practical applicability: Claims education/accessibility applications despite 49% accuracy being marginal for deployment. Acknowledged reliability concerns for L2 readers and those with cognitive impairments significantly limit real-world utility.
Incomplete baseline comparisons: Text-only baseline only in reconstruction task, not selection. No text+question baseline for selection as comparison point.

Presentation and scope concerns: Task setup artificial (given questions then paragraph). Multiple-choice with two questions sharing critical span creates contrived structure. Claim of 'arbitrary' goals overstated given constrained setting.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: First work to decode text-specific (semantic) reading goals from eye movements, with clear motivation for scientific and practical applications

Solid experimental design with large-scale dataset: 360 participants, 486 questions, 1M+ tokens; careful cross-validation accounting for non-iid structure; multiple evaluation regimes (New Text/Participant/Both); public dataset enabling reproducibility
Comprehensive evaluation framework: Multiple metrics for reconstruction quality; two task difficulty levels; multiple generalization regimes; thoughtful baselines
Clear presentation and ethical considerations: Well-organized paper with reproducibility details; thoughtful discussion of privacy concerns and deployment limitations
weaknesses: Modest performance improvements limit significance: Best model achieves 49.3% on All Spans (vs 33.3% chance); Same Span task shows only 57.3% vs 50% chance—incremental gains lacking compelling practical or scientific value

Weak reconstruction results and problematic evaluation: Question word Kappa only 0.069 in New Item regime; surface metrics show human questions outperforming model in New Text regime; heavy reliance on indirect QA accuracy metric (which depends on 86% accurate QA model); critically, no human evaluation of reconstruction quality

Limited modeling novelty: Discriminative models are existing architectures (Haller RNN, RoBERTEye-Fixations) simply adapted; generative models apply standard LLMs with LoRA fine-tuning; generative models underperform on primary selection task, undermining their contribution; no novel integration methods for eye movements

Insufficient analysis and interpretation: No error analysis or investigation of which question/reader types are harder; no ablation studies on eye movement features; missing feature importance analysis; no insight into what models actually learn; only one qualitative example provided

Dataset scope and generalization concerns: Only 486 questions/162 paragraphs in single domain (news, English-only); New Text & Participant regime uses only 1% of trials; constrained 3-way selection from overlapping questions limits ecological validity; unclear how findings generalize beyond this narrow setting

Unclear practical significance despite motivation: Claimed applications in education/assistive technology are not demonstrated to be feasible; 49-50% selection accuracy and very weak reconstruction fall well below deployment thresholds; ethical concerns about real-world use acknowledged but not resolved

Evaluation limitations: Question word and UIUC category metrics are too coarse-grained; BLEU/BERTScore have known limitations for generation evaluation; QA accuracy is indirect measure that could hide semantic differences; missing information-theoretic and simpler baseline comparisons; strong assumption in reading-time baseline not validated

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First to study text-specific open-ended goal decoding from eye movements (vs. procedural goal decoding in prior work)
Rigorous experimental design: Sophisticated cross-validation accounting for non-i.i.d. data, three generalization regimes, and two task difficulty levels
Comprehensive evaluation framework: Multiple metrics for reconstruction, informative baselines, extensive implementation details, and proper statistical testing
Strong results on selection task: 49.3% accuracy vs. 33% chance; notably 57.3% on harder 'same critical span' task vs. 50% chance, demonstrating fine-grained information extraction
Excellent generalization properties: Consistent performance across new texts, new participants, and both combined (Table 4-6)
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-written paper with sufficient detail, promises of public dataset release, and extensive appendices
Thoughtful ethical considerations addressing privacy, user identification, and fairness concerns
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Discriminative and generative models are straightforward adaptations of existing work; primary contribution is empirical rather than methodological

Weak reconstruction performance with concerning generalization: Question word Kappa drops from 0.478 (new participants) to 0.069 (new items); BLEU drops from 0.60 to 0.31. Substantial performance degradation suggests fundamental generalization challenges not adequately addressed
Unexplained model failures: DalEye-LLaVA performs at chance on selection (33.5%); simple RT-weighted baseline performs at chance despite theoretical motivation. These failures deserve investigation

Insufficient analysis and insights: No ablations showing which eye movement features drive performance, no error pattern analysis, no investigation of why 'same critical span' questions are harder, limited mechanistic understanding of what models learn

Limited scope and generalizability: Single language (English), single task format (OneStopQA), small dataset (~162 paragraphs). Unclear how findings transfer to other texts, languages, or reading scenarios. No participant demographic analysis

Evaluation design concerns: Using GPT-4o to categorize generated questions introduces circularity; QA accuracy metric is indirect and may credit plausible-but-wrong answers; distinction between log-likelihood and free-form generation evaluation is unclear

Practical limitations insufficiently addressed: 49.3% selection accuracy likely too low for reliable assistive technology; no computational cost analysis for 8.1B parameter models; no investigation of downstream application feasibility

Missing ablation studies and comparisons: No feature importance analysis, no exploration of alternative architectures, no simple statistical baselines (TF-IDF, word frequency), limited investigation of why theoretically-motivated baselines fail

strengths: Novel task formulation distinguishing semantic (text-specific) from procedural goal decoding, addressing an important understudied problem in reading comprehension and eye tracking research

Rigorous experimental design with proper train/test splits accounting for non-i.i.d. data structure and three meaningful evaluation regimes (New Participant, New Text, New Text & Participant) that meaningfully assess generalization

Comprehensive evaluation framework with multiple metrics, well-designed baselines (human incorrect questions, text-only variants, LLM arbitrary), proper statistical testing using mixed effects models, and thorough cross-validation
Valuable cognitive grounding (Figure 4) linking model performance to interpretable psycholinguistic features (reading times before/in/after critical spans), extending prior cognitive science findings
Exceptional reproducibility with extensive methodological documentation, hyperparameter details, detailed appendices, and promised code/data release
Strong performance on difficult same-critical-span task (57.3% vs 50% chance) demonstrates detection of fine-grained information-seeking distinctions
Comprehensive model comparison across discriminative and generative paradigms, including appropriate baseline models
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—discriminative models are straightforward adaptations of existing architectures (Haller RNN, RoBERTEye-Fixations), and generative models use standard LoRA fine-tuning. No novel architectures, training objectives, or eye movement representations

Moderate and fragile task performance: 49.3% on 3-way selection (16.3 points above chance), dramatic performance degradation on new texts for reconstruction (e.g., 67.4% → 54.5%), raising serious questions about practical utility and real-world applicability

Goal reconstruction task severely underdeveloped with poor generalization: BLEU scores ~0.56-0.64, only modest improvements over baselines, and substantial performance collapse on novel texts across all metrics. Paper acknowledges extreme difficulty but provides no path forward

Limited dataset scope severely restricts generalizability: only 162 paragraphs from single source (Guardian), narrow domain (news), single language (English), 486 total questions. Critical spans average 32 words (large portions of 109-word paragraphs), and questions derived from reading comprehension rather than natural information-seeking behavior

Insufficient failure analysis: no systematic investigation of when/why models fail, missing analysis of question type difficulty, no error categorization (semantic vs. surface errors). Anecdotal examples insufficient for understanding limitations

Poor performance of embedding-based approach (DalEye-LLaVA at baseline) inadequately investigated despite important implications for eye movement representation quality. Relegated to appendix with minimal discussion
Missing upper bounds: no human inter-rater agreement on goal selection or human performance ceiling for reconstruction, making it unclear whether achieved performance is meaningful
Feature ablation results (Table 13) show small effect sizes and substantial redundancy, suggesting eye movements may be noisier than hoped and that fixation ordering alone captures substantial signal

Ethical considerations underdeveloped: acknowledges potential biases for L2 readers and reading-impaired individuals but proposes no mitigation strategies; privacy implications of biometric data not adequately addressed

Unclear practical significance: proposed applications (e-learning, content personalization, assistive technology) remain speculative with no user studies or validation; current accuracy levels may be insufficient for real applications

strengths: Novel task formulation: Introduces a well-motivated distinction between procedural and semantic goal decoding from eye movements, addressing an understudied problem with scientific and practical value

Rigorous experimental methodology: Thoughtful data splits testing three generalization regimes (New Participant/Text/Both), proper statistical testing with mixed-effects models, and 10-fold cross-validation
Large-scale eye-tracking dataset: 360 participants, 1M+ word tokens, with careful critical span annotations enabling multiple evaluation perspectives

Meaningful cognitive analysis: Section 6.1 effectively links model performance to psycholinguistically interpretable features (reading times before/after/in critical spans), confirming theoretical predictions
Comprehensive evaluation: Multiple evaluation metrics for both selection (accuracy at different difficulty levels) and reconstruction (BLEU, BERTScore, QA accuracy, question type classification)
Reproducibility commitment: Detailed hyperparameters, data splits, training procedures, and promised code/data release; ethical considerations appropriately discussed
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Models are primarily adaptations of existing architectures (Haller RNN 2022, RoBERTEye 2024) without novel approaches tailored to this task's specific challenges

Severe and unexplained generalization failures: Performance on new texts drops dramatically (DalEye-Llama question word: 0.674→0.545, BLEU: 0.556→0.253, BERTScore: 0.776→0.631) without systematic investigation of causes or proposed solutions

Weak reconstruction results: Generated questions often underperform baseline 'Incorrect Human' questions on surface metrics, and text-only baselines are highly competitive, suggesting eye movements provide limited marginal benefit

Feature ablation undermines cognitive interpretation: Table 13 shows small performance drops when removing eye movement features, with the paper acknowledging most signal comes from fixation sequence ordering, contradicting heavy interpretation of Figure 4 coefficients as causal cognitive mechanisms

Circular evaluation for generation task: QA accuracy metric is only computable for 86% of examples where a QA model succeeds, introducing bias; furthermore, using QA model to validate reconstructions is circular if models share training distribution

Extreme sensitivity to input representation: Section G.2.3 shows word-level representations drop from 0.674 to 0.185 question word accuracy (73% decline), raising concerns about robustness and whether models learn meaningful representations

Task design limitations: Same Span variant (57.3% vs 50% chance) appears artificially constrained; candidate availability in selection task differs from real-world scenario; critical span annotations during training provide privileged information about task-relevant regions

Insufficient error analysis: Only one example (Table 16) provided across 486 test questions; no systematic investigation of which question types are harder to decode or why New Text generalization fails

Domain specificity and limited scale: 486 questions over 162 paragraphs in single-paragraph reading tasks (~5.8 sentences) from Guardian articles; unclear if findings transfer to longer texts, other domains, or languages
